Mattock
MAT-uk
noun
From the Old English mattuc, a broad-bladed hand tool for grubbing and breaking hard ground — part hoe, part pick, swung with both hands to loosen the soil, dig out roots, and clear the hillside for tillage.

Biblical Definition

The mattock is the labourer’s grubbing-tool, a heavy blade set crosswise on a haft and swung to break hard ground, dig out briers, and loosen the roots the plow cannot reach. Where the plow scores an open field, the mattock attacks the stubborn hillside and the thorn-choked corner by main strength of arm. Isaiah promises hills “that shall be digged with the mattock” (Isa 7:25), ground reclaimed foot by foot. Josiah carried mattocks through the cities of Manasseh and Ephraim (2Ch 34:6), breaking down the altars of the idols — the tool of tillage turned to reformation, for a land is cleared of idols as a hill is cleared of briers: by hard blows and no delicacy. But the word’s sharpest use is in the days of Saul. “Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1Sa 13:19); and so “all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock” (1Sa 13:20). Israel was disarmed, and worse: for the edge of every tool they owned they must go down to their enemies and pay their enemies’ price. A covenant people who cannot sharpen their own mattock will not long hold their own field. In the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of the people — the wage of dependence, collected at the worst hour.

Webster 1828 Definition

A heavy hand-tool with a broad blade, swung to grub up roots and break hard ground; part hoe, part pick.

MATTOCK, a tool to grub up weeds or roots; a broad-bladed pick for breaking hard ground.

From the Old English mattuc; part hoe and part pick, swung with both hands.

It reclaims the stony hillside the plow cannot reach (Isa 7:25).

Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his mattock (1Sa 13:20).

Josiah brake down the altars of the idols with mattocks (2Ch 34:6).

Key Scripture

1Sa 13:19 — "Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears:"

1Sa 13:20 — "But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock."

Isa 7:25 — "And on all hills that shall be digged with the mattock, there shall not come thither the fear of briers and thorns: but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen, and for the treading of lesser cattle."

2Ch 34:6 — "And so did he in the cities of Manasseh, and Ephraim, and Simeon, even unto Naphtali, with their mattocks round about."

Modern Corruption

A plain farm tool, and a live parable: a people who must go down to their enemies to sharpen their own instruments have already lost the field.

expand to see more

Here is a live corruption, and Israel’s mattock names it. The Philistines suffered no smith in the land, so that every man who would put an edge on his own tool must go down to his enemy and pay his enemy’s price. That is the picture of a church that borrows her instruments from the world — that takes her methods from the marketing house, her wisdom from the couch of the counsellor, her measure of success from the counting of crowds, and her courage from whatever the age will still applaud. The tool is Israel’s; the edge is the Philistine’s. And a man who must ask his enemy to sharpen his mattock will get exactly the edge his enemy wishes him to have — enough to till, never enough to fight. So it proved: in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of the people. The church that keeps no smith of her own will find, when the day of battle comes, that she has no weapon either.

The principle to recover is a forge within the camp. God has given His church her own smithy: the Scriptures, given by inspiration of God, that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works; the preached word; prayer; the ordinances; the discipline of a true church. These are edge enough for any ground. Josiah did not borrow Philistine tools to break down the altars of the high places; he took the mattocks of Israel and swung them. Let the church sharpen her instruments at her own anvil, upon the word of the living God, and the briers of the hillside will give way — for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a broad-bladed grubbing tool for breaking hard ground and digging out roots.

expand to see more

Mattock — from the Old English mattuc, a grubbing tool.

It is part hoe and part pick, swung by the arm to break hard ground.

It digs out the roots and briers the plow cannot reach (Isa 7:25).

Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen it (1Sa 13:20).

Josiah brake down the idols’ altars with mattocks (2Ch 34:6).

Usage

"The mattock breaks the ground the plow refuses: some soil yields only to the blow of the arm."

"Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his mattock — a people disarmed at the forge."

"Josiah swung mattocks against the altars: reformation is done with hard blows and no delicacy."
